lessons.title: The Ugali and Sukuma Wiki Puzzle — Launching the Anchoring Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: In the Predict activity, each learner fills in a Prediction Sheet about a lunch of ugali, sukuma wiki and nyama choma. Which is the best description of what you should write?
choices: One prediction only, about the food you like most
What you honestly think happens to each food after it is swallowed, including what you are not sure about
Only the facts the teacher has already taught, so that nothing is wrong
A copy of your partner's prediction, so that the class agrees
quiz.rationale: The Predict phase asks learners to write their own current thinking for each food, with a column for what they are unsure about. Predictions are not corrected and there are no wrong answers at this stage.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual Prediction Sheet (UGALI, SUKUMA WIKI, NYAMA CHOMA, WHAT I AM NOT SURE ABOUT)

quiz.prompt: During the 'Slow Look', learners must write only what they can observe on the NOTICE side of a card, without explaining. Which statement is an observation and not an explanation?
choices: The ugali is white, smooth and dense.
The nyama choma gives us protein.
The sukuma wiki is healthy for the body.
The ugali contains carbohydrates.
quiz.rationale: Colour, texture and structure can be seen directly, so this is an observation. The other statements are claims about nutrients or health that go beyond what is seen.
quiz.placement: Observe: 'Slow Look' and the NOTICE card

quiz.prompt: The teacher says: 'Your stomach is made of protein. Your stomach also produces acid and protein-digesting enzymes.' What puzzle does this raise?
choices: Why does the small intestine absorb nutrients into the blood?
Why does the stomach not digest itself?
Why does ugali digest faster than nyama choma?
How does the body know which digestive chemical to release, and when?
quiz.rationale: A stomach made of protein that also makes protein-digesting chemicals raises the puzzle of why it does not digest itself. This is one of the three anomalies recorded on the CANNOT YET EXPLAIN side of the card.
quiz.placement: Observe: three anomaly prompts, PUZZLE 3 (CANNOT YET EXPLAIN side of the card)

quiz.prompt: In the class gallery sort, the teacher reads out a prediction and counts the hand signals: 18 thumbs-up (we know this is true), 7 open hands (we think so) and 3 thumbs-down (no idea). Where does the teacher place that prediction?
choices: THINK SO, because some learners were unsure
It is taken off the board until the end of the unit
CONFIDENT, because most learners showed thumbs-up
NO IDEA, because some learners had no idea
quiz.rationale: The sticky note goes in the column chosen by the majority. 18 of the 28 learners gave thumbs-up, so it goes under CONFIDENT.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'What Do We Already Know?' gallery sort (CONFIDENT | THINK SO | NO IDEA)

quiz.prompt: In the gallery sort, the class looks for prior knowledge about each food that they are confident is true. Which matching of food and main component do learners describe as a visible part of the Kenyan meal?
choices: Ugali is mainly protein, sukuma wiki is mainly starch, and nyama choma is mainly fibre.
Ugali is mainly starch, sukuma wiki is mainly fibre, and nyama choma is mainly protein.
Ugali is mainly fibre, sukuma wiki is mainly protein, and nyama choma is mainly starch.
All three foods contain only starch.
quiz.rationale: Ugali (maize meal) is starchy, sukuma wiki (kale) is fibrous and nyama choma (grilled meat) is protein-rich. These are the three kinds of food matter in the meal.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'Known Foundation' identified in the gallery sort

quiz.prompt: On the Driving Question Board, a learner has a sticky note that says: 'Why does my stomach not digest itself?' Which colour of note does it belong on?
choices: No note. The teacher answers it straight away
Yellow: something I noticed about the meal
Blue: something I wonder or a question I have
Green: something I think I already know
quiz.rationale: Blue is for wonders and questions. Yellow is for observations and green is for things learners think they already know. Questions are collected, not answered, in this lesson.
quiz.placement: DQB: three-colour sticky notes (YELLOW noticed, BLUE wonder, GREEN know)

quiz.prompt: Learners label their first Food Journey Map 'DRAFT 1 — Before Investigation' and are told not to erase anything. Why?
choices: Draft 1 has to be correct so that it can be used as the final answer
It records their honest current thinking, so they can compare it with later drafts and see how their understanding changes
Mistakes must be hidden so that the final map looks perfect
The teacher will mark it and give a score for each correct part
quiz.rationale: The map is the first version of a model that will be revised in later lessons. Mistakes are treated as data that show where learning grows, so nothing is erased or marked.
quiz.placement: Model: first 'Food Journey Map' (DRAFT 1 — Before Investigation)

quiz.prompt: At the end of this lesson, the class has recorded 'Why is ugali digested faster than nyama choma?' as a puzzle. What is the status of this question?
choices: It was answered by the Driving Question card
It is an open question that has not been explained yet, and the class will investigate it during the unit
The teacher explained it during the gallery sort
The class voted and agreed on the answer
quiz.rationale: This lesson opens the inquiry and does not resolve any of the three puzzles. The question is recorded for investigation in later lessons.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: after the DQB and Food Journey Map, reflecting on the three puzzles

lessons.title: Mechanical vs. Chemical Digestion — Breaking Down the Ugali and Sukuma Wiki

quiz.prompt: Before the lesson, a learner predicts: "Teeth break the ugali into small pieces and that is all that happens in the mouth." Which statement best corrects this prediction?
choices: Chewing changes the starch in ugali into maltose
Saliva contains an enzyme that also chemically changes the starch in the mouth
Saliva only makes the food wet so it is easier to swallow
Chemical changes to food begin only in the stomach
quiz.rationale: Teeth only break food physically (mechanical digestion), but saliva contains salivary amylase which begins chemical digestion of starch in the mouth.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketch and 2-sentence prediction about what happens to ugali in the first 60 seconds in the mouth

quiz.prompt: A learner chews a plain piece of mandazi for 60 seconds without swallowing. The mandazi slowly starts to taste sweeter. What is the best explanation?
choices: Salivary amylase is changing starch in the mandazi into maltose, a sugar
Saliva is breaking down protein in the mandazi into sugar
The tongue adds sugar to the mandazi while mixing it
The teeth crush the mandazi and release sugar that was already in it
quiz.rationale: Mandazi is starchy. Salivary amylase in saliva chemically converts starch to maltose, which tastes sweet, so the sweetening is direct evidence of chemical digestion.
quiz.placement: Observe: the 'Mandazi Moment' demonstration (chewing for 60 seconds and recording taste at 20, 40 and 60 seconds)

quiz.prompt: While watching an animation of food moving from the mouth to the stomach, a learner records physical changes in the Observation Table. Which of these is an example of MECHANICAL digestion?
choices: Stomach wall muscles churning the food
Pepsin breaking down protein in nyama choma
Salivary amylase changing starch to maltose
Hydrochloric acid making the stomach acidic
quiz.rationale: Mechanical digestion is the physical breakdown of food, such as by teeth and stomach churning. Pepsin, HCl and amylase act chemically.
quiz.placement: Observe: animation of food moving from mouth to stomach, completing the Observation Table (physical vs chemical columns)

quiz.prompt: A learner chews ugali and it begins to taste sweet. Chewing nyama choma (grilled meat) does not make it taste sweet. What is the best reason?
choices: Ugali is softer than nyama choma, so the teeth can break it down more
Saliva only works on plant foods and not on animal foods
Salivary amylase acts on starch in ugali but not on the protein in nyama choma
Nyama choma is cooked so it has no chemicals that can change
quiz.rationale: Enzymes are specific. Salivary amylase breaks down starch (in ugali) but cannot act on protein (in nyama choma), like a jembe designed only for one job.
quiz.placement: Explain: group sentence answering 'Why did the ugali taste sweet after 60 seconds of chewing but the nyama choma would not?'

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the roles of pepsin and hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the stomach?
choices: Pepsin digests starch and HCl digests fats
Pepsin and HCl churn the food to break it into smaller pieces
Pepsin breaks down protein and it works only when HCl makes the stomach very acidic
HCl is an enzyme that digests protein and pepsin makes the stomach acidic
quiz.rationale: Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme that needs the acidic conditions made by HCl. Both act chemically, while churning is done by the stomach muscles.
quiz.placement: Explain: two-column chart of agents (salivary amylase, pepsin, HCl) and the lock-and-key / jembe analogy

quiz.prompt: In class, the teacher asks: "If pepsin and HCl break down protein, what stops the stomach from dissolving itself?" The teacher does not answer but puts it on the Driving Question Board. Why does this question arise from what learners have just seen?
choices: Because saliva from the mouth reaches the stomach and damages its walls
Because the stomach does not use any chemical digestion
Because the stomach makes HCl and pepsin, which break down protein, yet the stomach is part of a living body
Because mechanical churning in the stomach wears away its walls
quiz.rationale: Learners saw that the stomach produces strong acid and a protein-digesting enzyme. This raises the puzzle of why the stomach itself is not digested, which is left for a later lesson.
quiz.placement: DQB: cluster B question 'How the stomach avoids digesting itself'

quiz.prompt: When revising the 'food tube' model, a learner labels the stomach with [M], [C] or [M+C]. The stomach has muscular walls that churn food and gastric glands that release pepsin and HCl. Which label is correct for the stomach?
choices: [C] only, because the stomach only makes acid and enzymes
[M] only, because the stomach only churns the food
No label, because digestion starts and ends in the mouth
[M+C], because it churns food and also releases pepsin and HCl
quiz.rationale: Churning by the muscular walls is mechanical digestion and pepsin and HCl provide chemical digestion, so the stomach contributes to both.
quiz.placement: Model Building: revising the Lesson 1 'food tube' sketch with [M], [C] and [M+C] labels on the mouth, oesophagus and stomach

lessons.title: Enzymes and Regions of the Alimentary Canal — The Body's Chemical Toolkit

quiz.prompt: A research group fills in an enzyme chart for the mouth. Which row is correct for salivary amylase?
choices: Secreted by the stomach; acts on protein; produces peptides
Secreted by the salivary glands; acts on starch (for example in ugali); produces maltose
Secreted by the salivary glands; acts on starch; produces glucose only
Secreted by the pancreas; acts on fats; produces fatty acids and glycerol
quiz.rationale: Salivary amylase is made by the salivary glands and breaks starch into maltose. Glucose is only produced later, after further digestion in the small intestine.
quiz.placement: Observe: research groups construct the region-by-region enzyme summary chart (Region | Enzyme Name | Secreted By | Substrate | Product) for the Mouth

quiz.prompt: Lipase is an enzyme in the small intestine. What does lipase break down, and what does it produce?
choices: Peptides into amino acids
Fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Proteins into peptides
Starch into maltose
quiz.rationale: Lipase acts on fats (its substrate) and produces fatty acids and glycerol. Maltose comes from amylase, and peptides and amino acids come from protein-digesting enzymes.
quiz.placement: Observe: groups complete the Substrate and Product columns of the enzyme chart for the Small Intestine (pancreatic enzymes)

quiz.prompt: A learner eats a piece of nyama choma (grilled meat), which is rich in protein. Which statement correctly describes what pepsin does to it?
choices: Pepsin is made in the pancreas and breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Pepsin is made by the gastric glands and breaks protein directly into glucose
Pepsin is made by the gastric glands in the stomach and breaks protein into peptides
Pepsin is made in the mouth and breaks starch into maltose
quiz.rationale: Pepsin is secreted by the gastric glands, works in the stomach, and its substrate is protein. The product is peptides, not glucose or maltose.
quiz.placement: Explain: cold-called group (Group 2 – Stomach) explains what pepsin does to the nyama choma protein

quiz.prompt: Why can salivary amylase in the mouth not break down the protein in nyama choma?
choices: Because salivary amylase is made in amounts that are too small to work on any food
Because chewing destroys salivary amylase before it can act on protein
Because the mouth is too warm for any enzyme to work on protein
Because enzymes are specific: each enzyme acts only on its own substrate, and amylase acts on starch, not protein
quiz.rationale: Enzyme specificity means each enzyme acts on one type of substrate. Salivary amylase acts on starch, so protein needs a different enzyme such as pepsin or trypsin.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher's 5-minute consolidating explanation on why enzyme specificity matters (why salivary amylase cannot break down protein)

quiz.prompt: The mouth and stomach each have only one or two main enzymes, but the small intestine has many. What is the best explanation?
choices: Every enzyme in the small intestine breaks down all food types, but each one works slowly
The small intestine receives starch, proteins and fats, and each type of food needs its own enzyme
Enzymes in the mouth and stomach are used up, so the small intestine must replace them
The small intestine is narrow, so it needs more enzymes to push food along
quiz.rationale: Enzymes are specific to their substrates. The small intestine handles carbohydrates, proteins and fats from a mixed meal, so it needs a range of enzymes such as amylase, trypsin and lipase.
quiz.placement: Explain: cold-called question to Group 3 or 4 on why the small intestine needs so many different enzymes

quiz.prompt: When colour-coding an alimentary canal diagram, a learner uses one colour for protein-digesting enzymes. Which pair of enzymes should both be in that colour?
choices: Pepsin and trypsin
Pepsin and salivary amylase
Pancreatic amylase and pepsin
Lipase and trypsin
quiz.rationale: Both pepsin (stomach) and trypsin (small intestine) act on protein. Amylase acts on starch and lipase acts on fats.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the enzyme layer and colour-coded key (carbohydrate, protein, fat enzymes) to the cumulative alimentary canal diagram

quiz.prompt: In the small intestine, intestinal peptidases act on peptides that came from protein digestion. What is the final product of this step?
choices: Amino acids
Starch
Maltose
Fatty acids and glycerol
quiz.rationale: Intestinal peptidases break peptides into amino acids, the final products of protein digestion that can be absorbed into the blood.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: reviewing the completed enzyme chart for the Small Intestine (intestinal enzymes / brush border)

lessons.title: Food Tests Practical Part 1 — Detecting Starch and Reducing Sugars in Kenyan Foods

quiz.prompt: Before testing ugali, a learner recalls the enzymes from the last lesson. Which food substance does salivary amylase act on?
choices: Starch
Water
Fat
Protein
quiz.rationale: Salivary amylase digests starch, beginning in the mouth, and produces maltose. Protein and fat are digested by other enzymes.
quiz.placement: Predict: prediction card with Think-Pair-Share on ugali and ripe banana

quiz.prompt: A group tests a glucose solution as the control. What results should they expect?
choices: Iodine: blue-black; Benedict: stays blue
Iodine: brown-orange; Benedict: stays blue
Iodine: blue-black; Benedict: orange-red after heating
Iodine: brown-orange; Benedict: orange-red after heating
quiz.rationale: Glucose is a reducing sugar, not starch. Iodine stays brown-orange (no starch) and Benedict reagent turns orange-red when heated in a hot water bath.
quiz.placement: Observe: iodine test and Benedict test on the five food samples, including the glucose solution control

quiz.prompt: Raw maize flour turns blue-black when two drops of iodine are added. What does this result show?
choices: Starch is present in the maize flour even before it is chewed
Starch is absent from the maize flour
Reducing sugars are present in the maize flour
Salivary amylase has already digested the starch
quiz.rationale: Blue-black with iodine is a positive test for starch. Digestion by salivary amylase only starts when the food is chewed and mixed with saliva, so starch is still present in raw maize.
quiz.placement: Observe: iodine test comparing cooked ugali and raw maize flour

quiz.prompt: During the Benedict test, a test tube is heated in a hot water bath for five minutes. What is the safe way to handle the tube?
choices: Leave the tube in the boiling water bath and lift it out with your hand when the colour changes
Hold it with bare fingers so you can feel when it is hot enough
Use a test-tube holder and keep the tube at an angle, pointing away from your face and others
Hold it upright with a test-tube holder and look down into it
quiz.rationale: The tube is hot and its contents can spurt out. Use a holder and point the tube away from yourself and others.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher demonstration of Benedict test safety and heating in the hot water bath

quiz.prompt: A ripe banana gives an orange-red result with Benedict reagent, but an unripe banana gives a much weaker result. What best explains this?
choices: Benedict reagent detects starch, which is present in ripe bananas
Ripe bananas never contained starch at any stage
Iodine solution has changed the banana into sugar
During ripening, starch in the banana is converted into reducing sugars
quiz.rationale: As a banana ripens, its starch is changed to reducing sugars, so the Benedict test becomes positive and the banana tastes sweeter. Benedict reagent detects reducing sugars, not starch.
quiz.placement: Explain: group paragraph, prompt 2 (why ripe banana gives a positive Benedict result)

quiz.prompt: Cooked ugali gives a blue-black colour with iodine. Which is the best evidence statement to write in your notebook?
choices: Ugali contains no carbohydrate, because it does not taste sweet
Ugali contains starch, which is the substrate for lipase
Ugali contains starch, which is a substrate for salivary amylase and pancreatic amylase
Ugali contains reducing sugars, because starch and sugar are the same substance
quiz.rationale: Blue-black with iodine shows starch. Starch is digested by salivary amylase in the mouth and pancreatic amylase in the small intestine. Starch and reducing sugar are different substances, and lipase acts on fats.
quiz.placement: Explain: board evidence statement 'EVIDENCE FROM FOOD TEST — UGALI CONTAINS STARCH'

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a two-box diagram for ugali: Box 1 is MOUTH and Box 2 is SMALL INTESTINE. Which pair of labels is correct?
choices: Mouth: no digestion of starch happens; small intestine: salivary amylase digests all the starch
Mouth: salivary amylase breaks starch into maltose; small intestine: lipase digests the remaining starch
Mouth: pepsin breaks starch into maltose; small intestine: salivary amylase digests the remaining starch
Mouth: salivary amylase starts breaking starch into maltose; small intestine: pancreatic amylase digests the remaining starch
quiz.rationale: Starch digestion starts in the mouth with salivary amylase, which produces maltose. Any remaining starch is digested by pancreatic amylase in the small intestine. Lipase acts on fats, not starch.
quiz.placement: Model: two-box diagram (MOUTH and SMALL INTESTINE) using the ugali example

lessons.title: Food Tests Practical (Part 2) — Detecting Proteins and Fats in the Kenyan Meal

quiz.prompt: Before doing any tests, a learner predicts which nutrients are found in a cup of milk from the Kenyan meal samples. Which prediction is correct?
choices: Milk contains protein only, with no fat
Milk contains fat only, with no protein
Milk contains both protein and fat
Milk contains neither protein nor fat because it is a liquid
quiz.rationale: Milk is a familiar source of both protein and fat, so it should give a positive Biuret test and a positive ethanol emulsion test. Many learners wrongly think milk has no fat.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share prediction of protein-positive and fat-positive samples

quiz.prompt: In the Biuret test for protein, a learner puts 2 cm³ of bean broth in a test tube. Which sequence of steps is correct?
choices: Add 4–5 drops of copper sulphate solution first, then add dilute NaOH
Add absolute ethanol first, then pour into cold water
Add iodine solution first, then heat the tube in a water bath
Add dilute NaOH first, mix gently, then add 4–5 drops of 1% copper sulphate solution
quiz.rationale: NaOH is added first and then copper sulphate. Adding the reagents in the wrong order gives a false blue result instead of violet.
quiz.placement: Observe: Biuret test on the six labelled samples (NaOH first, then CuSO₄)

quiz.prompt: During the Biuret test, a group records a violet colour in the tube containing nyama choma extract. What should they conclude?
choices: Reducing sugar is present in the nyama choma
Fat is present in the nyama choma
Starch is present in the nyama choma
Protein is present in the nyama choma
quiz.rationale: A violet or purple colour with Biuret reagent is the positive result for protein. Starch, fat and reducing sugars are detected by other tests.
quiz.placement: Observe: recording Biuret results and the whole-class collated results table

quiz.prompt: In the ethanol emulsion test, a learner dissolves 2 cm³ of cooking oil in 5 cm³ of absolute ethanol. The learner then pours the solution into a test tube containing 5 cm³ of cold water. What result shows that fat is present?
choices: The mixture turns brick-red
The mixture turns milky white as an emulsion forms
The mixture turns blue-black
The mixture turns violet
quiz.rationale: Fat dissolves in ethanol but is insoluble in water. When the solution is poured into water, tiny fat droplets form a milky-white emulsion, which is a positive result.
quiz.placement: Observe: ethanol emulsion test on butter, cooking oil and the other samples

quiz.prompt: A learner is about to add absolute ethanol to a test tube during the ethanol emulsion test. What safety step must be done first?
choices: Put on a wet cloth so it can be used to blow out a flame if needed
Warm the ethanol gently over a flame so it dissolves the fat faster
Smell the ethanol closely to check that it is the correct liquid
Make sure no flame or spirit lamp is burning on the bench
quiz.rationale: Ethanol is flammable, so all flames on the bench must be out before it is used. Heating it or sniffing it closely is unsafe.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher safety demonstration and bench safety monitor check for flames

quiz.prompt: Nyama choma gives a strong violet colour with Biuret reagent. Which explanation of this colour change is correct?
choices: Copper ions react with starch molecules to form a violet complex
NaOH turns violet when it reacts with fat droplets
Copper ions coordinate with the peptide bonds in protein chains, producing the violet colour
Ethanol dissolves the protein and turns violet in water
quiz.rationale: In the Biuret test, copper ions coordinate with the peptide bonds in protein chains. More peptide bonds give a stronger violet colour.
quiz.placement: Explain: Question 1 – why nyama choma turns violet with Biuret reagent

quiz.prompt: Learners have shown that nyama choma is rich in protein. Which statement correctly links this to digestion in the stomach?
choices: Lipase in the stomach digests the protein into amino acids
Amylase in the stomach digests the protein at neutral pH
Pepsin, a protease, digests the protein, and the low pH of gastric acid activates it
Bile from the gall bladder digests the protein in the stomach
quiz.rationale: The stomach secretes pepsinogen, which is activated into pepsin by the acid (low pH). Pepsin is a protease that breaks protein into peptides.
quiz.placement: Explain: Question 2 – link between protein in nyama choma and pepsin

quiz.prompt: Cooking oil gave a positive ethanol emulsion test. Which statement about its digestion in the small intestine is correct?
choices: Bile salts emulsify the fat, and then lipase digests it into fatty acids and glycerol
Fat is digested in the stomach by pepsin before it reaches the small intestine
Lipase emulsifies the fat, and then bile salts digest it into fatty acids and glycerol
Bile is an enzyme that chemically digests the fat into fatty acids and glycerol
quiz.rationale: Fat is insoluble in water, so bile salts must first emulsify it into small droplets. Lipase can then digest it into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile is not an enzyme.
quiz.placement: Model: annotating the cumulative alimentary canal diagram at the small intestine (bile salts + lipase)

lessons.title: Adaptations of the Human Digestive System — Structure Meets Function

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 learner studies a diagram of one villus in the small intestine. Inside the villus is a network of tiny blood capillaries very close to the surface cells. What is the main advantage of this capillary network?
choices: It makes mucus to protect the villus from enzymes
It carries absorbed nutrients such as glucose into the bloodstream
It pushes food along the small intestine
It produces amylase to digest the starch from ugali
quiz.rationale: The capillary network inside each villus lets glucose and other nutrients that cross the epithelial cells enter the bloodstream straight away. Mucus comes from goblet cells, and enzymes are not made by capillaries.
quiz.placement: Observe: Evidence Table using the labelled villus cross-section (resource pack item A)

quiz.prompt: A learner says: "The small intestine absorbs all the nutrients from ugali, sukuma wiki and nyama choma because it is a very wide tube." The small intestine is actually only about 3 cm wide. Which statement gives the best structural explanation for how it absorbs so much?
choices: Its sphincters hold nutrients in the intestine for several days
Its villi and microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the surface area for absorption
Its strong hydrochloric acid breaks food into particles small enough to pass through
Its wall is made of very thick muscle that squeezes nutrients into the blood
quiz.rationale: Villi and microvilli multiply the absorptive surface area, so a 6 m tube absorbs as much as a far longer smooth tube would. The intestine is narrow, and hydrochloric acid is in the stomach, not the small intestine.
quiz.placement: Model: margin sentence answering how a 3 cm tube absorbs everything from the Kenyan meal

quiz.prompt: On the Driving Question Board, a group posts a GREEN card answering: "How does the stomach avoid digesting itself, even though it makes hydrochloric acid and pepsin?" Which answer is correct and complete?
choices: The stomach wall is covered by a mucus lining, and pepsin is released as inactive pepsinogen
Rugae fold away from the food so that acid never touches the wall
The stomach wall contains no protein, so pepsin cannot harm it
Pepsin works only in the small intestine, so the stomach never contains it
quiz.rationale: Mucus protects the stomach lining, and pepsin is released as inactive pepsinogen, so it only becomes active in the stomach's acid conditions. The stomach wall does contain protein, and pepsin acts in the stomach.
quiz.placement: DQB: GREEN cards for the question 'How does the stomach avoid digesting itself?'

quiz.prompt: When a learner eats a large meal of ugali and nyama choma, the stomach stretches and churns the food. Which structure of the stomach wall lets it expand and increases contact with the food during churning?
choices: Villi
Goblet cells
Rugae
Microvilli
quiz.rationale: Rugae are folds of the stomach wall that unfold to let the stomach stretch and increase the surface in contact with food for mechanical and chemical digestion. Villi and microvilli are in the small intestine, and goblet cells make mucus.
quiz.placement: Explain: annotating the stomach interior (rugae) on the Annotated Diagram Template

quiz.prompt: The cardiac sphincter is found where the oesophagus joins the stomach. What is its main role in digestion?
choices: It makes pepsinogen for protein digestion
It absorbs glucose from the stomach into the blood
It closes to stop stomach acid and food from flowing back up into the oesophagus (acid reflux)
It controls how quickly chyme leaves the stomach for the small intestine
quiz.rationale: The cardiac sphincter acts as a valve at the oesophagus-stomach junction and prevents acid reflux. Controlling the release of chyme is the job of the pyloric sphincter.
quiz.placement: Explain: labelling the cardiac and pyloric sphincters on the simplified alimentary canal diagram

quiz.prompt: During the class discussion the teacher asks: "What would happen if the pyloric sphincter opened too quickly and released half-digested chyme into the small intestine before enzymes had finished working?" Which answer shows the correct role of the pyloric sphincter?
choices: It makes the stomach wall fold into rugae
It keeps food in the oesophagus until the stomach is empty
It produces mucus that stops the stomach digesting itself
It controls the release of chyme from the stomach into the small intestine, so digestion is not rushed and can finish
quiz.rationale: The pyloric sphincter sits at the stomach-duodenum junction and releases chyme in controlled amounts, giving enzymes time to work. If it opened too quickly, digestion would be incomplete.
quiz.placement: Explain: whole-class discussion question about the pyloric sphincter opening too quickly

quiz.prompt: Ugali starch has been digested to glucose by amylase and maltase. Which path correctly shows how this glucose gets into the blood in the small intestine?
choices: It is absorbed by the rugae of the small intestine into the blood
It crosses the microvilli and epithelial cells of a villus into the capillary network inside the villus
It stays in the middle of the intestine and is carried out with the waste
It passes through the pyloric sphincter directly into the blood
quiz.rationale: Glucose is absorbed across the microvilli (brush border) and epithelial cells of the villus, then enters the capillary network inside the villus and is carried away in the bloodstream. Sphincters control movement of food and do not absorb, and rugae are in the stomach.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: Gallery Walk prompt 'trace the exact path glucose from the ugali starch takes into the bloodstream'

lessons.title: Model Building — Making a 3D Model of the Human Digestive System

quiz.prompt: A learner sketches the journey of a piece of ugali through the alimentary canal. Which sequence of organs is correct?
choices: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → large intestine → small intestine → rectum
Mouth → oesophagus → small intestine → stomach → large intestine → rectum
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum
Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine → rectum
quiz.rationale: Food passes from the mouth down the oesophagus to the stomach, then the small intestine, the large intestine and finally the rectum. The other options swap organs out of order.
quiz.placement: Predict Phase: individual sketch of the alimentary canal from memory

quiz.prompt: A group is writing its building list for the mouth. Which entry is correct for the enzyme and substrate in the mouth?
choices: Salivary amylase acts on proteins to form peptides
Lipase acts on fats to form fatty acids and glycerol
Salivary amylase acts on starch (as in ugali) to form maltose
Pepsin acts on proteins to form peptides
quiz.rationale: Salivary glands release amylase, which begins the chemical digestion of starch into maltose. Pepsin works in the stomach and lipase acts mainly in the small intestine.
quiz.placement: Observe Phase: Evidence Retrieval Gallery and building list (organ, process, enzyme + substrate)

quiz.prompt: A group is building its model and is asked: what does bile do to the fat in nyama choma, and why is that important?
choices: Bile carries digested fat across the villi into the bloodstream
Bile emulsifies fat into tiny droplets, giving lipase a larger surface to act on
Bile is an enzyme that chemically splits fat into fatty acids, so lipase is not needed
Bile is made in the stomach and digests the proteins in the meat
quiz.rationale: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It contains no enzymes, but it breaks large fat globules into small droplets so lipase can digest the fat efficiently.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: model construction, teacher probe on liver/bile entering the small intestine

quiz.prompt: A group labels the large intestine on its model. Which label is correct?
choices: Water is reabsorbed here; no digestive enzymes are made here
Pepsin digests proteins into peptides
Maltase and sucrase finish the digestion of sugars
Lipase digests the remaining fats
quiz.rationale: The large intestine mainly reabsorbs water from undigested food. It has no digestive enzymes, so a label without an enzyme is correct, not a mistake.
quiz.placement: Explain Phase: model construction, teacher probe on the large intestine with no enzyme labels

quiz.prompt: Damp sponge strips are placed inside the tube that represents the small intestine. What do these strips represent, and why do they matter?
choices: Bile, which breaks up fat into small droplets
Sphincters, which stop food from moving backwards
Stomach walls, which churn the food mechanically
Villi, which greatly increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients into the blood
quiz.rationale: The sponge strips model villi, the finger-like folds of the small intestine. They give a very large surface area, which explains how a tube only about 3 cm wide can absorb nutrients from a full school lunch.
quiz.placement: DQB Phase: selecting question cards the model answers, linking to the 3 cm tube puzzle

quiz.prompt: At the start of the unit, a learner said, "The stomach digests everything in our ugali, sukuma wiki and nyama choma." Which statement best shows where this idea is wrong?
choices: The stomach digests starch fully, so the small intestine only absorbs water
The stomach only stores food, and no digestion happens there
The stomach makes bile, so it digests fats but not proteins
The stomach starts protein digestion with pepsin and HCl, but most chemical digestion and nearly all nutrient absorption happen in the small intestine
quiz.rationale: In the stomach, churning, pepsin and HCl begin protein digestion only. Fats, starch and peptides are digested further in the small intestine, where villi absorb the nutrients. Bile is made in the liver, not the stomach.
quiz.placement: Model Phase: whole-class question, "where is the idea that the stomach digests everything wrong?"

quiz.prompt: A group adds a red 'Failure Mode' tag to the pancreas on its model. Which tag correctly describes what happens if the pancreas stops producing lipase?
choices: Starch in the ugali cannot be digested in the mouth
Proteins in the meat cannot be digested in the stomach
The fat in nyama choma is not digested and passes into the large intestine unabsorbed
The large intestine cannot reabsorb water from the waste
quiz.rationale: Lipase digests fats, and the pancreas supplies it to the small intestine. Without lipase, fat stays undigested and moves on unabsorbed. Starch digestion in the mouth, protein digestion in the stomach and water reabsorption do not depend on pancreatic lipase.
quiz.placement: Model Phase: 'Failure Mode' tag extension for groups that finish early

lessons.title: DQB Synthesis & Assessment — Driving Question Resolution and Unit Wrap-Up

quiz.prompt: A learner is doing Benedict's test on a sample. Which set of steps is in the correct order?
choices: Put about 2 cm³ of test solution in a test tube, add an equal amount of Benedict's solution and mix, place the tube in a hot water bath for a few minutes, then observe and record colour changes
Add Benedict's solution to a dry test tube, add a few drops of test solution, mix, and record the colour immediately without heating
Put about 2 cm³ of test solution in a test tube, place it in a hot water bath, then add Benedict's solution and record the colour once the tube is cold
Heat the Benedict's solution alone, add about 2 cm³ of test solution, then record the colour change without mixing
quiz.rationale: The four steps are: put about 2 cm³ of test solution in a tube, add an equal amount of Benedict's solution and mix, heat in a hot water bath for a few minutes, then observe and record all colour changes. Heating is required for the reaction, and mixing comes before heating.
quiz.placement: Observe: Benedict's test practical on the simulated 'digested ugali' sample (Steps 1–4)

quiz.prompt: After heating a glucose solution with Benedict's solution in a hot water bath, a brick-red precipitate forms. What does this result show?
choices: The solution contains a reducing sugar such as glucose
The solution has no sugar, because the blue colour has been lost
The solution contains protein, because Benedict's solution reacts with all nutrients
The solution contains starch, because starch turns Benedict's solution red
quiz.rationale: A brick-red (orange-red) precipitate is a positive result for reducing sugars such as glucose. Starch and proteins are not detected by Benedict's test, and a blue colour would mean no reducing sugar.
quiz.placement: Observe: Step 4 – observing and recording the colour change in the Benedict's test

quiz.prompt: In the practical, a dilute glucose solution was used to represent 'digested ugali'. Why is glucose a suitable choice to represent digested ugali?
choices: Ugali starch is already a reducing sugar, so it gives a positive Benedict's test before any digestion
Ugali contains mainly protein, and glucose is the end-product of protein digestion
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach turns starch into glucose within seconds
Amylase enzymes break the large starch molecules in ugali down into simple sugars such as glucose
quiz.rationale: Ugali is mostly starch. Amylase breaks starch down into maltose and then glucose, so digested ugali contains glucose, which Benedict's test can detect. Whole starch does not give a positive result.
quiz.placement: Observe: written question (a) – why the test solution represents digested ugali rather than whole ugali starch

quiz.prompt: Nyama choma is rich in protein. Which statement correctly matches the enzyme pepsin to its region of action and substrate?
choices: Pepsin acts in the mouth and breaks down starch into maltose
Pepsin acts in the small intestine and breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Pepsin acts in the stomach and breaks down starch into glucose
Pepsin acts in the stomach and breaks down proteins into smaller peptides
quiz.rationale: Pepsin is secreted in the stomach, works in the acidic conditions there, and breaks proteins such as those in nyama choma into smaller peptides. Starch is digested by amylase and fats by lipase.
quiz.placement: Explain: pairs' written answer to the driving question – naming enzyme-region matches with correct substrates and products

quiz.prompt: In the Explain phase, pairs wrote about what happens when an adaptation of the digestive system fails. Infection with the bacterium H. pylori can damage the mucus lining of the stomach. Why can this lead to an ulcer?
choices: The stomach starts to digest starch, which burns a hole in the wall
The villi in the stomach are destroyed, so nutrients cannot be absorbed
The stomach can no longer make any acid, so food stays undigested and forms a sore
The wall of the stomach loses its protection and is damaged by the acid and pepsin in the stomach juice
quiz.rationale: The mucus lining protects the stomach wall from hydrochloric acid and pepsin. When H. pylori damages the mucus, the wall is exposed and gets damaged, forming an ulcer. This also links to the puzzle of how the body avoids digesting itself.
quiz.placement: Explain: sentence on what happens when an adaptation fails (e.g. ulcers caused by H. pylori disrupting the stomach's mucus lining)

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki, ugali and nyama choma are broken down into small soluble molecules. How do the villi and microvilli of the ileum help the body absorb these nutrients efficiently?
choices: They make the intestine wall thick so that nutrients cannot escape back into the food
They grind the food into smaller pieces so it can pass through the intestine wall
They increase the surface area of the intestine wall, so more nutrients can be absorbed into the rich network of capillaries
They release hydrochloric acid to dissolve the nutrients so they can enter the blood
quiz.rationale: Villi and microvilli greatly increase the absorbing surface area of the ileum. Each villus has a rich capillary network that carries absorbed nutrients away in the blood.
quiz.placement: Model Building: comparing the Lesson 1 journey map with the Lesson 7 3D model – linking to model label 'villi'

quiz.prompt: A learner's Lesson 1 sentence said, 'Enzymes break down food.' Which upgraded sentence is the most scientifically complete?
choices: Enzymes in the mouth and stomach help to break down food into smaller parts.
Pepsin in the mouth breaks down the proteins in ugali.
The mouth breaks down ugali when we chew it with our teeth.
Salivary amylase in the mouth begins to break down the starch in ugali into maltose.
quiz.rationale: A complete sentence names the enzyme, where it acts, the substrate and the product: salivary amylase, mouth, starch in ugali, maltose. The other options are vague or wrongly matched (chewing is mechanical digestion, and pepsin works in the stomach).
quiz.placement: End of lesson: after the Model Building final sentence 'The human digestive system is adapted … because…' and the journey map upgrades
